agenda_text:
CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK
  THE CITY COUNCIL ACTING ON BEHALF OF THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY OF THE FORMER
 REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY, THE HOUSING AUTHORITY, THE MONTEREY PARK FINANCING
  AUTHORITY AND THE MONTEREY PARK GEOLOGIC HAZARD ABATEMENT DISTRICT
  AGENDA

  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MONTEREY PARK CITY HALL COUNCIL CHAMBERS
  320 W. NEWMARK AVENUE, MONTEREY PARK, CA 91754

  Wednesday
  September 18, 2024
  6:30 p.m.

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up to 24 hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov or by completing an online
form at www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

[3.]  CONSENT CALENDAR ITEM NOS. 3A-3J
  All items under the Consent Calendar are considered by the City Council to be routine and will
  be enacted by one motion. Specific items may be removed from the Consent Calendar at the
  request of any member of the City Council for separate consideration.

3-A.  MONTHLY INVESTMENT REPORT – AUGUST 2024
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Receiving and filing the monthly investment report; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-B.  CONSIDERATION AND POSSIBLE ACTION TO ADOPT THE 2024 CONFLICT OF
  INTEREST CODE FOR THE CITY OF MONTEREY PARK IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE
  POLITICAL REFORM ACT
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting the resolution amending the City's Conflict of Interest Code; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-C.  APPROVAL OF AN AMENDMENT TO THE AGREEMENT WITH CIVICPLUS LLC FOR A
  NEW AGENDA AND MEETING MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Authorizing the City Manager to execute an amendment to Agreement No. 1775-A with
  CivicPLus, LLC, in a form approved by the City Attorney, to provide an Agenda and
  Meeting Management Software for an amount not to exceed $60,000 for the term ending
  July 31, 2028;
  (2) Authorizing the Finance Director to appropriate $12,908.60 from the Administration -
  General Fund to the FY2024-25 Budget.
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  Page 2 of 287
   Monterey Park City Council Agenda, September 18, 2024 - Page 3

3-D.  2024 BANNED BOOKS WEEK RESOLUTION
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a resolution declaring the week of September 22-28, 2024 as Banned Books
  Week in Monterey Park,
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-E.  2024/2025 CANNABIS TAX FUND GRANT PROGRAM (CTFGP) FUNDING FOR TWO LAW
  ENFORCEMENT MOTORCYCLES
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Waiving bidding requirements pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Codes §3.20.050
  (2) through (4), and authorizing the City Manager to execute an amendment to Agreement
  No. 2004-A with Long Beach BMW Motorcycles, in a form approved by the City Attorney,
  for the purchase of two (2) 2024 BMW R1250 RT-P 753 law enforcement motorcycles;
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-F.  AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE AN AGREEMENT WITH THE
  GREETINGS TOUR AND ARTIST VICTOR VING IN A FORM APPROVED BY THE CITY
  ATTORNEY FOR A COMMUNITY MURAL PROJECT FOR AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED
  $40,000
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Authorizing the City Manager to negotiate and execute an agreement, in a form approved
  by the City Attorney, with the Greetings Tour and artist Victor Ving for a community mural
  for an amount not to exceed $40,000;
  (2) Providing direction on the process for final art and location selection; and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-G.  EMERGENCY REPLACEMENT OF THE HVAC SYSTEM AT THE LANGLEY SENIOR
  CITIZEN CENTER– ADOPT A RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO
  EXECUTE NECESSARY AGREEMENTS, WITHOUT THE NEED FOR COMPETITIVE
  BIDDING TO COMPLETE THE HVAC REPLACEMENT
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute necessary Agreements,
  not to exceed $75,000, without the need for competitive bidding to complete emergency
  replacement of the HVAC system at the Langley Senior Citizen Center
  (2) Appropriating $75,000 to the FY 2024-2025 Budget from the General Fund for the project;
  and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  This matter is categorically exempt from review under the requirements of the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to 14 California Code of Regulations § 15269
  (emergency repair to this public facility is necessary to maintain service essential to the public,
  health and welfare) and § 15301 (Existing Facilities). The extended repairs would result in minor
  alterations to existing public facilities involving no significant expansion of the existing use. The
  project is not anticipated to have any significant impacts with regard to regarding traffic, noise,
  air quality, or water quality. There are adequate utilities and public services to serve the project.
  Additionally, the City Council’s actions are exempt from additional CEQA review as they are
  being made to protect public and private property and necessary to maintain services essential
  to the public, health and welfare (see, CalBeach Advocates v. City of Solana Beach (2002) 103
  Cal.App.4th 529: CEQA findings regarding an anticipated imminent emergency are valid).

  Page 3 of 287
   Monterey Park City Council Agenda, September 18, 2024 - Page 4

3-H.  BRUGGEMEYER LIBRARY IMPROVEMENTS – AUTHORIZE PURCHASE OF 26 NEW
  HVAC UNITS FROM CARRIER CORPORATION
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Waiving the bidding requirements pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code §
  3.20.050(4), and authorizing the City Manager to execute a contract with Carrier
  Corporation, in a form approved by the City Attorney, not to exceed the listed cost per
  Council’s selected Option A, B or C to purchase 26 New HVAC Units for the Bruggemeyer
  Library;
  (2) Authorizing the Director of Public Works to approve change orders and contingency up to
  $10,000; and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the extension under the California Environmental
  Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated
  thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guidelines
  §§ 15060(c)(2), 15061(b)(3), and 15378 exempt activities that will not result in a direct or
  reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment, activities where there is
  possibility that it may have a significant effect on the environment, and activities that do not
  constitute a “project” as defined, respectively. This activity contemplates purchasing equipment
  only. Subsequent installation and construction will be evaluated separately under CEQA.
  Accordingly, this activity is exempt from further review.

3-I.  FIRE STATION 63 UPGRADES AND REMODEL
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a Resolution to add Fire Station 63 upgrades and remodel to the Fiscal Year
  2024-25 Capital Improvement Program;
  (2) Appropriating $2 million in State funds for the proposed Capital Improvement Project; and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-J.  RUSSELL RESERVOIR 1A REHABILITATION PROJECT – AWARD OF PUBLIC WORKS
  CONTRACT TO CROSNO CONSTRUCTION INC.
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Authorizing the City Manager to execute a public works contract, in a form approved by
  the City Attorney, with Crosno Construction Inc. in the contract amount of $2,168,516 for
  the Russell Reservoir 1A Rehabilitation Project;
  (2) Authorizing the Public Works Director to approve change orders not to exceed $325,277
  over the total contract amount;
  (3) Authorizing the City Manager to execute a Professional Services Agreement, in a form
  approved by the City Attorney, with SA Associates in the contract amount of $120,000 for
  Project Support Services for Russell Reservoir 1A Rehabilitation Project; and
  (4) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Ordinance pursuant to the
  California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and
  the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). CEQA Guideline § 15301(c) (Existing Facilities) exempts the operation, repair,
  maintenance, alteration of existing public or private structures which involve negligible or no
  expansion of existing or former use. The proposed work will occur entirely within an existing
  structure. Accordingly, no further environmental review is required.

   Monterey Park City Council Agenda, September 18, 2024 - Page 5

[4.]  PUBLIC HEARING

4-A.  A PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER APPROVAL OF THE CONSTRUCTION AND
  SUBDIVISION OF AIR RIGHTS FOR A 64-UNIT CONDOMINIUM DEVELOPMENT
  (“PROJECT”) ON THE REAL PROPERTY LOCATED AT 338 – 410 SOUTH ALHAMBRA
  AVENUE, ALSO IDENTIFIED BY ASSESSOR’S PARCEL NUMBERS 5259-004-036, 5259-
  004-037, AND 5259-004-038
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Opening the public hearing and taking testimonial and documentary evidence;
  (2) Receiving documentary and testimonial evidence;
  (3) Closing the public hearing;
  (4) After considering the evidence received during the public hearing for the construction and
  subdivision of air rights for a 64-unit condominium development: (1) adopting a resolution
  to adopt a Mitigated Negative Declaration (“MND”) (State Clearing House Number
  2024051026) and approving Tentative Map No. 84188 (“TM-23-05”), Design Review
  (“DRB-23-105”); and (2) introducing and waiving the first reading of an ordinance
  approving Development Agreement (“DA-23-03”) ; and
  (5) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the Project pursuant to the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). An initial study was prepared in accordance with the CEQA Guidelines § 15063
  (“IS”) which shows that, if mitigated, the Project would not cause any significant environmental
  impacts. Accordingly, pursuant to CEQA § 21091, the City prepared a Mitigated Negative
  Declaration (“MND”) of environmental impacts for the Project. Based on the IS findings, and with
  proposed mitigation measures for air quality, biological resources, cultural resources, geology
  and soils, and noise, the Project would not result in significant environmental impacts.

  The IS, MND and a notice of intent to adopt the MND was prepared, circulated, and made
  available for public review between Thursday, May 23, 2024, and Wednesday, June 12, 2024.
  During this period, the City received 32 comments in support of the project and 35 comments
  protesting the project. While many of the comments received did not include CEQA related
  issues, those that did were evaluated and incorporated into the MND as appropriate. Accordingly,
  no further environmental review is required.

[5.]  NEW BUSINESS – None.

[6.]  CITY COMMUNICATIONS (CITY COUNCIL)

6-A.  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK, CALIFORNIA, IN
  SUPPORT OF MEASURE G FOR A MORE ACCOUNTABLE, TRANSPARENT, AND
  REPRESENTATIVE LOS ANGELES COUNTY GOVERNMENT (REQUESTED BY MAYOR
  WONG)
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a Resolution of the City Council of Monterey Park, California, in support of
  Measure G for a more accountable, transparent, and representative Los Angeles County
  government; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING OCTOBER 2024 AS DOMESTIC
  VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH (REQUESTED BY COUNCIL MEMBERS SANCHEZ AND
  LO)
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a Resolution of the City Council of Monterey Park, California, declaring and
  recognizing October 2024 as Domestic Violence Awareness Month; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

6-C.  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY PARK,
  CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING OCTOBER 3, 2024, AS LATINA EQUAL
  PAY DAY (REQUESTED BY COUNCIL MEMBER SANCHEZ)
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting a Resolution of the City Council of Monterey Park, California, declaring and
  recognizing October 3, 2024, as Latina Equal Pay Day; and
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  DATE: September 18, 2024

  TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
  FROM:  Maychelle Yee, City Clerk
  SUBJECT:  Consideration and possible action to adopt the 2024 Conflict of Interest
  Code for the City of Monterey Park in accordance with the Political
  Reform Act

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting the resolution amending the City's Conflict of Interest Code; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Pursuant to the Political Reform Act, Government Code § 81000, et seq., every local
agency is required to review its Conflict of Interest Code disclosure biennially to determine
if the Code is accurate or in need of amendment. City staff has reviewed its previous
determinations relating to disclosure levels and determined that Resolution No. 2022-R77
should be amended to include revisions consistent with existing positions in the City.

BACKGROUND:

On June 5, 2024, the City Council directed the City Clerk to review the City’s Conflict of
Interest Code in accordance with Government Code § 87306.5. A review of the City’s
2022 Conflict of Interest Code shows that changes are desirable as set forth below and
in the accompanying draft resolution.

In developing a disclosure list for the conflict of interest code, a designated employee or
commissioner is an officer, employee, member or consultant of an agency whose position
is designated in the code because the position entails the making or participation in the
making of governmental decisions, which may foreseeably have a material effect on any
financial interest (Government Code § 82019).

Making a governmental decision, means the person: (1) votes on a matter; (2) appoints
a person; (3) obligates or commits his or her agency to any course of action; or (4) enters
into any contractual agreement on behalf of his or her agency.

Participating in the making of a decision, means the person: (1) negotiates, without
significant substantive review, with a governmental entity or private person regarding the
decision; or (2) advises or makes recommendations to the decision-maker by conducting

  Page 11 of 287

research or an investigation, preparing or presenting a report, analysis or opinion which
requires the exercise of judgment on the part of the employee and the employee is
attempting to influence the decision.

It should be stressed that this action does not relieve any public official, employee, or
designated consultant following any and all state statutes governing conflict of interest or
regulations promulgated by the Fair Political Practices Commission. This action is only
an attempt by the City to appropriately notify the public of potential areas where a conflict
may foreseeably arise in the course of these individuals carrying out their normal duties
through public disclosure.

The following amendments are recommended:

  •  Adding new positions:
  o Media Supervisor
  o Senior Code Compliance Officer
  o Assistant Water Utility Manager

  •  Removing positions:
  o Members of the Personnel Board
  o Apprentice Fire Inspector
  o Support Services Manager
  o Support Services Supervisor

  •  Revising titles of existing positions:
  o Economic Development Manager/Economic Development Project
  Manager to Economic Development Manager
  o Division Chief to Battalion Chief
  o Fire Inspector to Fire Safety Specialist
  o Code Enforcement Officer to Code Compliance Officer
  o Management Services Department to Finance Department
  o Director of Management Services to Director of Finance
  o Financial Services Manager to Finance Manager
  o Director of Public Works/City Engineer to Director of Public Works
  o Assistant City Engineer to City Engineer

  •  Moving positions to accurately reflect the organizational chart as adopted in the
  2024-25 City Budget :
  o Deputy City Clerk from the Office of the City Clerk to the Office of the City
  Manager
  o Economic Development Manager and Economic Development Specialist
  from the Office of the City Manager to Community Development
  Department

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute an amendment to Agreement No. 1775-
  A with CivicPLus, LLC, in a form approved by the City Attorney, to provide an
  Agenda and Meeting Management Software for an amount not to exceed $60,000
  for the term ending July 31, 2028;
  2. Authorizing the Finance Director to appropriate $12,908.60 from the Administration
  - General Fund to the FY2024-25 Budget.
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
CivicPlus, LLC currently manages the city’s website. Staff recommends an amendment
to Agreement No. 1775-A to add an Agenda and Meeting Management Software to assist
staff with the drafting, routing, and creation of agenda packets for both City Council and
Commission/Board meetings. The proposed system will also provide enhanced features
such as a voting system and assistance with the preparation of meeting minutes.

BACKGROUND:
City staff had reviewed the product demonstrations of the agenda management systems
from its current document depository/public document portal provider, GRM Document
Management and its current website provider, CivicPlus, LLC. In evaluating the two
solutions, staff considered the needs of the city which included customized staff report
and agenda templates, methods for convenient agenda modifications, efficient
management of agenda packets, and a well-organized automated routing and approval
process.

After evaluation of the two products, GRM’s software did not meet all the criteria and had
a higher initial start-up cost. CivicPlus’s software meets the needs of the city while also
providing a component for a Live Meeting Manager; a feature which migrate agenda
contents, records official actions and discussions into a meeting minutes template. The

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Monterey Park Bruggemeyer Library is observing the week of September 22-28,
2024 as Banned Books Week. Banned Books Week is observed nationwide annually in
the fall to celebrate the freedom to read, highlight the value of free and open access to
information and spotlight current and historical attempts to censor books in libraries and
schools.

The theme for Banned Books Week 2024 is “Freed Between the Lines.” Readers can find
freedom in the pages of a book — but book bans and censorship threaten that freedom.
This Banned Books Week, everyone is encouraged to celebrate the right to read and the
freedom found in books. Libraries offer opportunities for everyone, regardless of race,
ethnicity, creed, ability, sexual orientation, gender identity, or socio-economic status, to
explore new worlds and become their best selves through access to information,
technology, multimedia content, and educational programs.

 SUBJECT:  Authorizing the City Manager to execute an agreement with the
  Greetings Tour and artist Victor Ving in a form approved by the City
  Attorney for a community mural project for an amount not to exceed
  $40,000.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Authorizing the City Manager to negotiate and execute an agreement, in a form
  approved by the City Attorney, with the Greetings Tour and artist Victor Ving for a
  community mural for an amount not to exceed $40,000;
  2. Providing direction on the process for final art and location selection; and
  3. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City Council has expressed interest in public art in the City of Monterey Park. In an
effort to learn more about the various options available and provide the Council with
options to consider, the Director of Recreation & Community Services researched and
met with various artists who specialize in working with cities on mural projects that
promote civic pride and promote local economic development.

Staff from the City Manager’s Office and the Recreation & Community Services
Department recently met with local San Gabriel Valley artist Victor Ving. Victor is the
owner and entrepreneur of the Greetings Tour Project (www.greetingstour.com) and has
been touring the Country to work with communities and develop murals that are visually
captivating and culturally significant. The murals help celebrate each city’s unique
heritage, landmarks, and community spirit.

On Tuesday, August 20, the Community Participation Commission (“CPC”) reviewed the
Greetings Tour website and murals that Victor Ving has completed in other cities. The
Commissioners were excited to learn about the opportunity to have a mural celebrating
the Monterey Park community. The CPC voted unanimously to recommend that the City
Council pursue a Greetings Tour postcard-style mural at a location to be determined.

Upon approval and providing direction on the process for final art and location selection,
city staff will work with artist Victor Ving to initiate community engagement, set a project
timeline, and scout potential public and private locations. The proposed mural project will
include community engagement and collaboration, ensuring it reflects the city's identity

  Page 78 of 287
 Staff Report
September 18, 2024

and values. The mural would be strategically placed in a high-visibility area, making it
accessible to residents and creating a destination for visitors.

If approved, updates will be provided as the project progresses. Once artwork has been
determined and location has been selected, the outcome will be presented to City Council
to request a budget allocation and final mural approval.

BACKGROUND:
The Greetings Tour is a nationwide public art project led by muralist Victor Ving and
photographer Lisa Beggs. The project specializes in creating postcard-style murals that
reflect the unique character of each city it partners with. The Greetings Tour has
successfully completed similar projects in various cities across the United States, creating
a new destination and local landmark in each community.

The Greetings Tour mural project presents a unique opportunity to showcase the City’s
unity and create a lasting visual legacy. City Council direction on this project will enable
staff to proceed with planning and initiate community engagement toward the final mural,
reflecting pride in the past and faith in the future.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The total project cost may vary due to the location and final design of the mural but will
not exceed $40,000. The funding source will depend on the location selected for the
mural. Development Impact Funds (“DIF”) may be utilized if the mural will be placed in a
city park; CDBG funds may be used if the location area meets the income requirements;
or the General Fund will be used if the location doesn’t meet the DIF or CDBG
requirements.

  What made you decide to do this project?
  The Greetings from Chinatown mural in NYC (2014) was the first piece we did where we noticed the potential of how much our artwork can positively affect the

with Westco for $34,249 and with Carrier Global Corporation for $ 28,730.74.

BACKGROUND
On September 4, 2024, Public Works staff determined that the HVAC system at the
Langley Senior Citizen Center was not operating correctly. Staff requested maintenance
support from Westco for the system. Westco performed necessary repairs for continued
operation. The HVAC unit services the main room used for daily senior lunch program
and public events. Additionally, the Langly Senior Citizen Center is a designated cooling
center. With the recent heat, this has proven to be a vital service to our community.
Despite the City’s best efforts, the system is beyond repair, and even with the temporary
fix it is operating at 50% capacity and can fail at any time. The system has exceeded its
expected lifespan of 10 to 15 years and is now 19 years old.

Staff obtained a quote from Carrier Global Corporation for one Packaged Rooftop Heat
Pump Unit and curb adapter for $28,730.74 and a quote from Westco for installation of
equipment for $34,249.

Westco’s scope of work includes providing a crane and removal and disposal of the
existing unit; installation of the City provided Carrier AC rooftop package unit, including
all electrical and control wiring; securing the unit to the existing platform; starting and
testing. The total cost for the proposed work is $34,249.

Ordinarily, the City must comply with this project's competitive bidding requirements of
the Monterey Park Municipal Code and Public Contracts code. However, due to the
immediate need to respond to the failing HVAC unit, competitive bidding for the proposed
replacement would be ineffective and impractical for the protection of public health and
safety. Westco is already vetted by City staff and under contract for HVAC maintenance
and will perform the work within the competitive unit prices listed in the existing
maintenance agreement.

Staff requests the City Council adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute
the necessary Agreements, not to exceed $75,000, with Carrier Global Corporation and
Westco without the need for competitive bidding for the emergency replacement of the
HVAC system at the Langley Senior Citizen Staff requests the appropriation of $75,000
for costs associated with this project including labor, material, permit, contingency, and
construction management and inspection.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The proposed Resolution supports the City’s strategic goal to maintain, build and
modernize infrastructure and facilities to support the current and future needs of the City
and community. Replacement of the HVAC unit is required for public health and safety.

FISCAL IMPACT
Staff recommends the appropriation of $75,000 to the FY 2024-2025 Budget from the
General Fund to cover the costs for this project.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Bruggemeyer Library HVAC units have reached the end of their useful service life
and are due for replacement. Capital Improvement Project (“CIP”) No. 95038 – Building
Forward Library Facilities Improvements Program allows for the replacement of the City
library’s HVAC units. Staff recommends the City Council authorize the City Manager to
purchase 26 HVAC units from Carrier Corporation based on one of the options identified,

BACKGROUND:
Bruggemeyer Library hosts approximately 800 to 1,000 visitors per day and is one of the
City’s designated cooling centers during extreme heat weather conditions. After decades
of prolonged use, the Library’s HVAC units have reached the end of their useful service
life and require replacement. Through the receipt of grant funds in January 2024 from the
California State Library, the City is able to move forward with The Building Forward Library
Facilities Improvements Program, which allows for the replacement of 26 HVAC units at
Bruggemeyer Library.

Through Sourcewell Contract # 070121-CAR, effective October 7, 2021, between
Sourcewell and Carrier Global Corporation, Carrier Corporation was able to present an
equipment quotation to the City for 26 HVAC units with Sourcewell pricing. The City is a
member of Sourcewell, a purchasing cooperative that combines the purchasing power of
multiple agencies into a cooperative purchasing group to secure lower prices than what
a smaller agency may obtain through an individual bid. Sourcewell contracts are
competitively solicited and meet public bidding requirements; accordingly, the City
Council may authorize the purchase of 26 HVAC units via MPMC § 3.20.050(4) - which
allows the City to forego bidding through a purchasing cooperative.

Based on City Council’s request at the August 21st meeting to evaluate all electric options,
staff contacted Carrier Corporation and electrical contractors to evaluate this option.
Based on the information and quotes gathered, the following options are available for the
City Council to make a decision:

  •  Option A (in-kind replacements) – This option would replace the existing units
  with the electric and natural gas option. These units are more efficient than the
  current units and will still have a reduction on greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).
  The current cost for this option is $342,436

  •  Option B (hybrid of in-kind and all electric replacements) – This option would
  focus on replacement of units with all electric units that do not need any additional
  infrastructure retrofit work. Currently, there are 12-units that would meet this
  requirement. The estimated cost for this option is $353,067

  •  Option C (all electric replacements) – This option would replace all electric and
  gas units with only electric units. The current estimated cost would be
  approximately $511,000. For this option, additional funding would be needed as
  there is not enough funding in the grant and matching funds to complete all of the
  work identified in the grant.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The replacement of the HVAC units at the Bruggemeyer Library supports the City’s goal
to maintain City facilities to support the current and future needs of our city and
community. Additionally, the project will allow for the library to continue to be a designated
cooling center during extreme heat weather conditions.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The proposed purchase will be made through grant funds from the California State
Library, Grant Number BF-23-004 budgeted under CIP No. 95038 – Building Forward
Library Improvements. There are sufficient funds in CIP 95038 to purchase the proposed
in-kind equipment or hybrid of in-kind and all electric equipment, plus contingency amount
not to exceed $10,000.00. However, should the all-electric option be approved,
approximately $150,000 will need to be allocated from the general fund to support this
decision. Once the full installation cost is sent out for bid, staff will bring back the item for
City Council to approve and allocate the funding.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council

 SUBJECT:  Fire Station 63 Upgrades and Remodel

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a Resolution to add Fire Station 63 upgrades and remodel to the Fiscal
  Year 2024-25 Capital Improvement Program;
  2. Appropriating $2 million in State funds for the proposed Capital Improvement
  Project; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
In October 2023, Assemblymember Mike Fong announced he had secured $2 million in
funding from the California 2023-24 State budget for the reconstruction of Fire Station 63.
The state funds will be used for the design, demolition and reconstruction of Fire Station
63.

BACKGROUND:
Built in 1958, Fire Station 63 is one of the oldest fire stations in the San Gabriel Valley.
Due to its age, Fire Station 63 is beginning to exceed its useful life and does not meet the
needs of a modern fire department. Over the years, the station has experienced some
damage from earthquakes, resulting in cracked floors and shifts in the foundation, which
pose a safety issue for staff. Similarly, the building was constructed over 66 years ago,
and needs modernized accommodations, such as gender-inclusive showers, restrooms
and living quarters.

Staff estimates the Fire Station 63 upgrades will be a multi-year project, similar to the
recently completed Fire Station 62. The money from Assemblymember Mike Fong will
assist staff in the design, and project management portion of the project, as well as
partially assist with the construction portion. Based on the cost of Fire Station 62’s design,
management, construction, and including inflation, staff estimates the total cost of Fire
Station 63 upgrades to be between $6 and $7 million. The total cost of the project is
dependent on various factors such as design requirements, staff relocation, site-specific
conditions and construction costs. Knowing there is a gap in funding, staff will be looking
for other sources of funding to ensure the project is completed.

Density Bonus
A Density Bonus is proposed as part of this Project and is a mechanism established by
California law that allows developers to obtain concessions and/or waive local
development requirements in exchange for building affordable housing.

The High-Density Residential land use designation of the General Plan allows 30 units
per acre. The Property is approximately 1.73 acres; accordingly, 51.9 units are permitted
by the General Plan at 30 dwelling units per acre, before considering Density Bonus law.
The proposed 64-unit housing development with a density of 37.5 units per acre is less

Since the Project designates 15% of the units as restricted to very-low incomes
households, the City is mandated by California law to grant a minimum of three incentives
that allow the Applicant to avoid certain development standards that it retains discretion
to choose. As part of the density bonus, the applicant has requested that incentives be
provided to the following areas, consistent with the MPMC §21.18.050:

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The proposed project is a 64-unit mixed-market rate and affordable housing development
(the “Project”). The Project is located on the east side of Alhambra Avenue, at the easterly
terminus of Peach Street, between Newmark Avenue and Graves Avenue on the real
property located at 338 – 410 South Alhambra Avenue (the “Property”). Properties within
the vicinity of the Property include other one and two-story multi-unit residential
developments constructed in the 1950s through 2018.

According to Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) Chapters 21.44 and 21.18, the
mixed-market rate and affordable housing development may be permitted through a
Development Agreement and Density Bonus. Additionally, the Applicant is requesting
approval of a tentative map to subdivide the Project’s air-rights for condominium purposes

  Page 264 of 287
 to enable the sale of each unit separately. The Project is designed according to the
MPMC, is consistent with the allowed density, and provides affordable and market rate
housing units consistent the City’s adopted Housing Element.

The Project was scheduled for a public hearing before the City Council at its Special
Meeting on June 18, 2024. At the meeting, the City Planner briefly presented her
recommendation to continue the public hearing to allow finalization of the Project’s
development agreement. During the public hearing and following testimony from the
community regarding the scale of the Project, and concerns related to public safety,
traffic, and parking impacts, the City Council determined that the Project would be better
served by allowing the City’s Planning Commission to further study these issues and
referred the Project to the Planning Commission for recommendation.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the Project pursuant to the California
Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
Guidelines”). An initial study was prepared in accordance with the CEQA Guidelines §
15063 (“IS”) which shows that, if mitigated, the Project would not cause any significant
environmental impacts. Accordingly, pursuant to CEQA § 21091, the City prepared a
mitigated negative declaration (“MND”) of environmental impacts for the Project. Based
on the IS findings, and with proposed mitigation measures for air quality, biological
resources, cultural resources, geology and soils , and noise, the proposed development
would not result in significant environmental impacts.

The IS, MND and a notice of intent to adopt the MND was prepared, circulated, and made
available for public review between Thursday, May 23, 2024, and Tuesday, June 12,
2024. During this period, the City received 32 comments in support of the project and 35
comments protesting the project. While many of the comments received did not include
CEQA related issues, those that did were evaluated and incorporated into the MND as
appropriate. Accordingly, no further environmental review is required.

TYPE OF ACTION (LEGISLATIVE; QUASI-JUDICIAL; OR ADVISORY)

Advisory: In considering approval of the proposed project, the Planning Commission is
acting as an advisory body to the City Council. Approval of the project is within the
authority of the City Council because it includes a Development Agreement and related
approvals pursuant to MPMC § 2.56.020(c).

Planning Commission’s recommendation to the City Council, however, plays an important
role in the approval process and should include the factual and legal basis for the Planning
Commission’s findings. The City Council can then consider those findings when making
its own determination.

Planning Commission’s recommended action to City Council is to approve and adopt a
TM, DRB, DA, and associated Mitigated Negative Declaration. In considering such
actions, the Planning Commission acts in a quasi-judicial role. In doing so, the Planning

  Page 265 of 287
 Commission acts like a court: it applies facts gathered during a public hearing to existing
law. Just like a court, the Planning Commission can only consider facts that are relevant
to the case. A party appearing before the legislative body is entitled to:

  •  Notice of the proposed action;

  •  Reasons for the action;

  •  A copy of the evidence on which the action is based; and

  •  The right to respond before a reasonably impartial, non-involved reviewer.

The Planning Commission must base its decision upon substantial evidence within the
record. “Substantial evidence” generally means enough relevant information and
reasonable inferences from information gathered during a public hearing that a fair
argument can be made to support a conclusion, even though other conclusions might
also be reached. Argument, speculation, unsubstantiated opinion or narrative, evidence
which is clearly erroneous or inaccurate, or evidence of social or economic impacts does
not constitute substantial evidence. Substantial evidence includes facts, reasonable
assumptions predicated upon facts, and expert opinion supported by facts. If the Planning
Commission asks irrelevant questions and bases its decision-making on such questions,
a court may overturn the Planning Commission’s decision and potentially hold the City
liable for violating the applicant’s constitutionally protected due process rights.

To recommend approval of the TM (per MPMC § 20.04.070), the Planning Commission
must find that the project is:

  •  Consistent with the Monterey Park General Plan;

  •  Consistent with any applicable specific plan or planned development;

  •  Consistent with the provisions of the MPMC;

  •  In the interest of public health and safety; and

  •  A necessary prerequisite to the order development of the surrounding area.

To recommend approval of the Design Review (per MPMC § 21.36.060), the project must:

  •  Be compatible and in keeping with the character of the neighborhood and not
  detrimental to the general welfare of the neighborhood in which they are located;

  •  Reflect the values of the community; enhance the surrounding environment; and
  harmonize with its surroundings; and

  •  Provide a visually pleasing setting for structures on the site through landscaping.

BACKGROUND

The Applicant is requesting approval of TM-23-05, DRB-23-105 and DA-23-03 for the
subdivision of air rights to construct a 64-unit mixed market and affordable housing
condominium project at 338-410 South Alhambra Avenue. The Property is zoned R-3
(High-Density Residential) and has a General Plan designation is High Density
Residential. The Property is currently developed with multi- and single-family residential
dwelling units and is surrounded by residential properties on all sides (see Figure 1).

  Page 267 of 287
 Figure 1: Project Site Aerial – 338-410 S. Alhambra Avenue

Site and Architectural Design

The Project is designed with two housing product types that total 64 multi-family
residential dwelling units: (1) seven townhomes; and (2) 57 stacked condos. The frontage
along Alhambra Avenue of the Project will feature seven attached townhomes that have
front entries along Alhambra Avenue. Behind the row of townhomes will be a larger
building that features the balance of the 57 condominium units, common open space and
parking facilities (see Figure 2). The townhomes are three levels, with parking at ground
level and the living areas two stories above. Because the Property slopes down from the
street, when viewing from the street, the townhome units appear two-stories, but feature
a bermed landscape front setback, leading to front entries that are slightly elevated from
the street level. The larger condominium building will be at the rear with three stories of
living units and common open spaces over a subterranean parking garage.

Parking and Circulation

The Project will be accessible from Alhambra Avenue by two driveways, one at the north
end and one at the south end of the Property. These two driveways will have a U-
configuration around the townhome units, so each unit is able to access its own two-car
garage. The northerly driveway will span almost the full depth of the Property and provides
a single point of ingress and egress to the parking garage area for the condo units in the
rear building.

  Page 268 of 287
   Total parking spaces proposed for this Project is 97. Each townhome will feature
  individual two-car garages (14 total garage spaces). Additionally, subterranean parking is
  provided for the condominium units at the rear of the Property, which is proposed to
  contain 83 standard parking spaces.

  The Applicant proposed parking at a ratio that is higher than State Density Bonus law and
  did not invoke lower applicable parking ratios that allow for ½ a parking space for units
  that are in close proximity to high quality transit as found on Garvey Avenue,
  approximately 0.3 miles to the north. A comparison of parking requirements and proposed
  parking is detailed in the table below. Figure 2 shows the site plan for the Project
  containing the outline of the proposed buildings, access points and landscape areas.

  As part of the requirements of this Project, the City requested and reviewed a Focused
  Traffic Analysis of the site and the surrounding neighborhood. While the Project screens
  below the City’s established Vehicle Miles Traveled (“VMT”) policy thresholds and does
  not have an impact to transportation under to CEQA, there is acknowledgement that there
  may be potential impact to on-street parking along Alhambra Avenue and Peach Street,

  Page 269 of 287
 with areas surrounding both the multi-family and single family-homes potentially being
used for overflow parking. Because the Project meets and exceeds the State’s Density
Bonus parking ratio, the City cannot require additional parking of this Project.

However, to help provide safe access to and from the Property, staff is requiring a strategy
to help maintain some on-street parking along the project’s frontage. Off-site
improvements will include the installation of a 20’ red curb to the south of the northernmost
driveway and 20’ of red curb to the north of the southernmost driveway, which will allow
cars to see around parked vehicles and to safely exit project driveways while still providing
some on-street parking. A condition of approval has been added to the project conditions.

The architectural design of the Project includes a contemporary style of architecture,
combining clean lines, simple building forms such as a flat roof with a parapet. a mix of
wall finishes including stucco, concrete, wood siding, and windows with dark trims.
Recessed balconies and front entries are located along the Alhambra Avenue elevation,
and the use of large windows help break up the massing and scale of the Project. The
neutral color palette is subdued with white stucco, gray accent walls, and light wood trims.
The mix of textures are understated, but contribute to the overall clean and uncluttered
appearance (see Figure 3 – West Elevation)

Figure 3: West Elevation (facing Alhambra Avenue)

The Project is designed to fit into the neighborhood and surrounding properties through
its compliance with the required setback requirements which provide adequate buffers to
existing adjacent developments. The following setbacks are provided between the
proposed development and adjacent properties:

  •  North of project site: 26-foot-wide setback is provided to the detached, 2-story,
  townhome development;

   •  South of project site: 10-foot setback is provided to the 3-story townhome

To soften the development’s appearance on the street (west) elevation, the townhomes
bring the scale of the Project down as the density of the project transitions between the

in the rear building, that will include amenities such as seating areas and dining areas
that are attractively landscaped. Staff recommends the inclusion of a barbecue area and

approval. Other common open space areas will be located on all levels of the

Tentative Map (“TM”)

The Property is comprised of three lots totaling 75,386 square feet (1.73 acres). The
Applicant proposes to reconfigure the three lots into one lot and simultaneously subdivide
the Property for air rights for each dwelling unit. The subdivision allows separate
ownership of each dwelling unit (persons own the air space of a particular dwelling, while
all the condominium owners mutually own and are responsible for all maintenance of the
buildings and the common areas).

The proposed TM is consistent, in terms of density and use, with the MPMC and General
Plan designations. The Property is zoned for multiple-family residences and the General
Plan allows for a density between 16.1 and 30 dwelling units per acre. The Project
proposes 64 residential units on approximately 1.73 acres which is rough 51.9 units per
acre. While this figure is higher than contemplated in the General Plan, the Project is
utilizing and consistent with the Density Bonus law and, accordingly, the Project does not
exceed the maximum density allowed under the General Plan (see discussion below
regarding Density Bonus).

plans, and proposed conditions of approval. Pursuant to MPMC Chapter 20.10, the

California law that allows developers to obtain concessions and/or waive local

per acre. The Property is approximately 1.73 acres; accordingly, 51.9 units are permitted

A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK, CALIFORNIA, IN
SUPPORT OF MEASURE G FOR A MORE ACCOUNTABLE, TRANSPARENT, AND
  REPRESENTATIVE LOS ANGELES COUNTY GOVERNMENT

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. The governance structure of Los Angeles County has remained unchanged since
  1912, a time when the population was approximately 500,000 residents and before
  women were granted the right to vote.

  B. Today, Los Angeles County is the most populous county in the nation, with over
  10 million residents, and is served by only five elected supervisors, each
  representing approximately two million constituents.

  C. The current structure limits the ability of the Board of Supervisors to be fully
  responsive to the diverse needs and challenges faced by communities across the
  County.

  D. Reforming Los Angeles County’s governance structure is necessary to address
  the region’s most pressing issues and to ensure a County government that is truly
  accountable, transparent, and representative.

  E. Measure G, a comprehensive governance reform package, has been placed on
  the November 2024 ballot by the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors on
  July 30, 2024.

  F. Measure G proposes to create an independent Ethics Commission, establish the
  position of an elected County Executive, and expand the Board of Supervisors,
  among other reforms.

  G. The establishment of an independent Ethics Commission will enhance
  transparency, build public trust, and combat corruption within the County’s
  governance.

  H. The creation of an elected County Executive will provide necessary checks and
  balances, improve the efficiency of County operations, and ensure that the
  management of the County’s budget is accountable to the public.

  I. Expanding the Board of Supervisors from five to nine members will allow for more
  diverse voices to be heard and will increase the accessibility of Supervisors to the
  communities they represent.

  Page 282 of 287
 Resolution No.
Page 2 of 2

  J. Additional reforms in Measure G include the creation of a commission to review
  the County Charter every ten years, the establishment of a Department of Budget
  and Management and a County Legislative Analyst, the requirement for open
  budget hearings by departments annually, and the formation of a task force
  comprised of members of the public to oversee the implementation of these
  reforms.

  K. Measure G represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to bring necessary
  structural changes to Los Angeles County’s government and to ensure that it can
  effectively address issues such as homelessness, public safety, social services,
  and meaningful public engagement.

  L. The City of Monterey Park stands with the communities of Los Angeles County in
  calling for a government that is more accountable, transparent, representative, and
  that is capable of effectively addressing the challenges of the 21st century.

  M. The City of Monterey Park strongly supports Measure G and urges the voters of
  Los Angeles County to approve these critical reforms on the ballot in November
  2024.

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. October 3, 2024, is Latina Equal Pay Day. We recognize the wage gap that Latina
  women face as part of a broader set of disparities that Latina women encounter in
  homeownership, unemployment, poverty, access to childcare, and the ability to
  accumulate wealth.

  B. Latinas are one of the fastest-growing, most influential groups in the United States.
  Latinas excel in every sector and industry in our country.

  C. Latinas make up the second largest group of women workers in the United States
  at 13,900,000 workers nationwide. One in five people in the State of California is
  Latina.

  D. Latinas continue to face the pay gap that is, on average, 51 cents to every dollar
  paid to white, non-Hispanic men. The wage disparity reflects the economic hurdles
  Latinas continue to encounter.

  E. More than twelve million Latinas account for 17.57% of the female labor force, a
  figure that is projected to grow dramatically, according to the Bureau of Labor
  Statistics.

  F. Nearly 4 in 10 mothers are primary breadwinners in their households, and nearly
  two-thirds of mothers are the primary or significant earners, making pay equity
  critical to the economic security of their families.

  G. A lifetime of lower pay means women have less income to save for retirement and
  less income counted in a Social Security or pension benefit formula. Latinas lose
  $1,200,000 in potential earnings on a 40-year career.

  H. Due to the wage gap, Latinas in California would have to work until 116 years of
  age to earn what a White non-Hispanic male earns by 60 years of age.

  I. The wage gap is a disadvantage for Latinas, their families, and the economy, and
  fair pay in California would strengthen the security of individuals and families today,
  regardless of education or socioeconomic status, while enhancing our statewide
  economy.

   J. Until the women who perform some of the most essential jobs can achieve
  economic security, our economy and communities will not be as strong as they
  possibly can be.

  K. The Monterey Park City Council hereby proclaims October 3, 2024, as Latina
  Equal Pay Day in recognition of the need to eliminate the gender gap in earnings
  by women and to promote policies to ensure equal pay for all.

  AND SUBDIVISION OF AIR RIGHTS FOR A 64-UNIT CONDOMINIUM
  DEVELOPMENT (“PROJECT”) ON THE REAL PROPERTY LOCATED AT 338
  – 410 SOUTH ALHAMBRA AVENUE, ALSO IDENTIFIED BY ASSESSOR’S
  PARCEL NUMBERS 5259-004-036, 5259-004-037, AND 5259-004-038.

  The proposed project is a 64-unit mixed-market rate and affordable housing
  development on the real property located at 338 – 410 South Alhambra Avenue
  (the “Property”) and includes the construction of seven townhomes at the front of
  the Property and a rear building containing 57 stacked condominium units. By
  developing seven units affordable to very-low income households, the Project is
  able to utilize State density bonus law, including incentives, to increase the number
  of units that can be built which contributes towards the City’s Regional Housing
  Needs Assessment (“RHNA”).

  This item was heard after Agenda Item No. 3F
   72-239
  September 18, 2024
CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the Project pursuant to the
California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.
“CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§
15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). An initial study was prepared in
accordance with the CEQA Guidelines § 15063 (“IS”) which shows that, if
mitigated, the Project would not cause any significant environmental impacts.
Accordingly, pursuant to CEQA § 21091, the City prepared a Mitigated Negative
Declaration (“MND”) of environmental impacts for the Project. Based on the IS
findings, and with proposed mitigation measures for air quality, biological
resources, cultural resources, geology and soils, and noise, the Project would not
result in significant environmental impacts.

The IS, MND and a notice of intent to adopt the MND was prepared, circulated,
and made available for public review between Thursday, May 23, 2024, and
Wednesday, June 12, 2024. During this period, the City received 32 comments in
support of the project and 35 comments protesting the project. While many of the
comments received did not include CEQA related issues, those that did were
evaluated and incorporated into the MND as appropriate. Accordingly, no further
environmental review is required.
